The problem with current AI security
Probabilistic AI cannot defend deterministic infrastructure.
The commercial generation of AI-assisted security tools shares three failure modes that make them unsuitable for regulated or OT deployment:
Probabilistic false positives. Cloud-based ML models routinely produce false alarms. In OT environments where downtime cascades into operational failure — fuel distribution, warehouse automation, logistics infrastructure — false-positive-driven automatic response is unacceptable.
Cloud dependency. Most commercial AI security agents require cloud connectivity for model inference. This is incompatible with air-gapped OT segments, classified networks, and any environment where data sovereignty is non-negotiable.
Black-box decisioning. Probabilistic LLM-based detection cannot be audited at per-decision granularity. For environments where every authorization decision must be defensible to oversight — OIG, GAO, DoD — black-box detection is a compliance liability.
“The unsolved problem: an AI-assisted security system that is deterministic, air-gappable, auditable per-decision, and precise enough to enable autonomous response.”

From passive to active defense
Zero false positives isn't a metric. It's what makes autonomous response possible.
The reason AI security has remained passive — detect and alert, never autonomously respond — is that no system has been precise enough to trust with automatic action. BETHANY changes that equation.
Where the industry is today
Passive defense
Detect anomalies. Generate alerts. Route to human analyst. The analyst decides. The attacker moves faster than the workflow.
Detect — probabilistic ML flags potential threat
Alert — event logged, analyst notified
Wait — human reviews, decides, acts
Respond — minutes to hours after detection
Where BETHANY is going
Active defense
Deterministic detection enables autonomous response. Zero false positives means you can trust the system to act — because it has never acted when it shouldn't have.
Detect — deterministic cascade fires at sub-2ms
Attribute — per-layer audit trail written locally
Respond — autonomous action within the response window
Learn — Jean hardens detection for every future encounter automatically
Coming next — Jean learns social engineering
Network-layer defense can't see what Jean can.
A credentialed insider being walked into an exfiltration sequence. An external attacker conducting reconnaissance through authorized interaction channels. These attacks don't cross the network perimeter — they walk through it with a badge.
Jean is being extended to detect social engineering at the interaction level — before it becomes a network event. Jean observes behavioral signals in real time, distinguishes adversarial probing from legitimate queries, and hardens its recognition with every encounter. Early validation: 60% per-turn social engineering detection from a 0% baseline, at sub-millisecond latency. This is Phase II scope — named here because the threat is real now.

Why this matters
Two results that tell the whole story.
Refusing impossible tasks is as important as completing possible ones
Four tasks were designed to be physically impossible — targets out of reach, eyes too small for the gripper. Jean refused all four, with specific reasons each time.
A system that claims success on impossible tasks is dangerous. The integrity of any physical AI system depends on its ability to recognize and name its own limits. Jean does this — and it does it without being told in advance which tasks are impossible.
Zero false successes is the integrity guarantee
Across all runs, Jean never reported a success it did not physically earn. No optimistic reporting, no partial completion counted as full success, no ambiguous result called a win.
In physical systems — industrial automation, surgical assistance, defense applications — a false success can cause real harm. The zero false success record is not a nice-to-have. It is the precondition for deployment in any high-stakes environment.
How Jean reasons about physical space
Jean's reasoning ran inside the control loop. Placement decisions, perception of the workspace, inverse kinematics selection, and rigid-body physics were provided by the simulation stack (ROS 2, MoveIt 2, Gazebo). Jean supplied the reasoning layer — deciding which grasp to attempt, how to adjust for precision, and when to refuse.
This is not a robotic arm trained on robot demonstrations. There is no training data. No learned policy. No neural network. The same deterministic reasoning engine that decides whether a student's lesson plan is complete decides whether a gripper approach is viable. Substrate changes. Engine doesn't.

How Jean controls the arm
Three decisions. All deterministic.

Grasp selection
Jean evaluates the target — geometry, accessibility, tolerance — and selects a grasp approach. Deterministic scoring, not probability sampling. Jean can explain why it chose the approach it did.

Precision adjustment
Jean adjusts for the gap between the planned approach and the physical constraints of the target. On standard tolerance, this runs at sub-1mm accuracy. On fine tolerance, the current boundary is named below.
03
Refusal with reason
When a task is physically impossible, Jean refuses — and names the reason. Out of reach. Eye too small. Gripper clearance insufficient. The system knows what it doesn't know.
The honest boundary — named, diagnosed, fix specified
Fine-precision threading (0.4mm eye) is not yet achieved.
On fine-tolerance trials, Jean's reasoning was correct every time — the grasp selection and precision adjustment decisions were right. The arm missed because a goal-pose correction was expressed in a link frame that rotates under the alternate IK configuration MoveIt selects for the fine pose.
This is a diagnosed motion-planning limitation, not a reasoning failure. The fix is specified: closed-loop visual servoing (perceive → correct → retry) eliminates the dependency on the static goal-pose expression. That is the next build milestone.
We report this boundary explicitly because the result that survives a hostile reader is the only result worth showing. A system that hides its limits cannot be trusted with its successes.

What this evaluation tests
One engine. A new substrate.
Jean was built to close the educational achievement gap. Its architecture is a deterministic mathematical reasoning stack, not a trained model. The architectural claim — validated across education, cybersecurity, clinical reasoning, sensor fusion and robotic manipulation — is that the same engine generalises across substrates without being rebuilt for each.
This SIL tests that claim in a substrate with properties the robotics work did not have: a continuously acting disturbance, a plant that must be characterised before it can be controlled, and a task where the correct answer is sometimes to do nothing.
The edge of a SIL
A SIL stops at the edge of the physical world by definition.
What it can prove is whether the decision and control logic is sound against an independent world. What it cannot prove is real-hardware performance — a separate, later category.
Architecture under test
Jean retained only the decision layer.
Everything she reasoned about was provided by independent, non-authored software.
Independent — not authored by Jean
Physics and hydrodynamics: Gazebo Harmonic, with the DAVE/REXROV work-class ROV model. Jean never received ground truth about forces.
Sensors: simulated DVL, depth, pressure and IMU, published through a ROS 2 bridge Jean did not write.
Actuation: the vehicle's own wrench interface.
Jean's layer
POWELL — fusion quality
CFADS — authority assessment
BARCA — response selection
RANDOLPH — intervention timing
The regulator is deterministic and stays deterministic. Jean decides whether to intervene, at what authority, and at what moment; a PID executes. This mirrors the robotics SIL, where CARVER selects the grasp and MoveIt executes it. Jean does not compute inverse kinematics there and does not compute PID arithmetic here.

sections.heading: Formulas need a currency.
sections.summary: The integration finding  The most transferable result of this evaluation is not a number. Jean's formula stack is deliberately agnostic about units — the formulas are a structure for comparison.
sections.text:
The integration finding
Formulas need a currency.
The most transferable result of this evaluation is not a number.
Jean's formula stack is deliberately agnostic about units — the formulas are a structure for comparison. But a comparison requires a common currency, and the integration must supply it.
Four successive architectures failed on this point before the fifth worked. Each used dimensionless weights and costs, so their ratios were arbitrary:
Hold cost 0.02 against CorrectSoft's 0.18 — a 10× denominator advantage chosen by nothing. Hold won from every state: 3 639 of 3 639 samples.
Decision margins of 0.01 logged as reasoning when they were coin flips.
The fix was to denominate everything in newtons, because that is what the actuator speaks and what the plant model is written in:
value_N = P × (force avoided later) − (force spent now)
Holding is not free — the deviation persists and grows, so the force needed later is larger. Correcting spends force now to avoid spending more later. That is a genuine economic comparison, and its margin means something.
This principle generalises to any application where the formula stack meets a physical system.

sections.summary: Where it actually broke  01 An upstream defect in a published research model DAVE's REXROV model gives each thruster joint the same <pose> as its child link. Since SDF joint poses are child-relative, each revolute axis sat ~1.1 m from its …
sections.text:
Where it actually broke
Every defect was at an interface.
01
An upstream defect in a published research model
DAVE's REXROV model gives each thruster joint the same <pose> as its child link. Since SDF joint poses are child-relative, each revolute axis sat ~1.1 m from its thruster and the links orbited as the propellers spun. Runtime geometry disagreed with the model by up to 1.64 m and 153°.
Patched, verified to 0.000°, and disclosed in code comments rather than silently worked around.
02
The actuation interface
The vehicle's persistent-wrench topic accumulates: every message stays applied. A controller publishing each cycle therefore applied the running sum of its entire command history — roughly 8 000 wrenches over a 300 s run. The instantaneous topic applies for one physics step, so at controller rates the force acts for under 1% of the time.
The workable pattern is to publish the delta against a tracked standing value. The accumulation that broke two days of work became the mechanism that made continuous force possible.
03
Reset transients caused three separate failures
set_pose teleports position and orientation but not velocity. Every run inherited momentum from whatever preceded it. This produced: unexplained Gate 2 variance; a 354% spread across three runs of an identical binary; and, in Phase 3, run 1 having more command updates than run 2 in every trial — 586 vs 81, 1250 vs 456, 920 vs 177.
Recorded in full — the test that lied
Our own harness reported a pass it hadn't earned. We caught it by reading the numbers.
The first version of our Phase 0 test harness printed "PHASE 0 PASSED." It was wrong. The vehicle had reportedly risen under downward force, and the total response across a 1,200 N swing was a rounding error — but the monotonicity check passed on noise that happened to be ordered. Two entirely different transports produced deltas of 0.0564 and 0.0548 — the same artifact.
"A gate that passes when it should not is a more serious defect than the bug it was built to catch."
Three defects: no minimum effect size, a detection threshold below the natural variation in the vehicle's buoyant drift, and a baseline measured at a different depth than the test. None of it was caught by the test. It was caught by a person reading the numbers and asking why a vehicle rose when pushed down.
The second false result
A Phase 1 diagnostic reported drag at 11 272% of applied force, because it differentiated two adjacent samples at 10 Hz. It reported 4.00 m/s where the true average was 0.14 m/s.
Standing consequence: every gate criterion must state a minimum effect size, not only a direction or an ordering.
We record this because it is the whole discipline: an instrument that has never been caught failing has not yet been tested. The constants this program now runs on superseded the earlier assumed values by factors of 55×, 26×, and 1,500×. Every one of those corrections came from refusing to trust a green checkmark.

sections.text:
Read this before anything else you quote
This is a SIL. No physical hardware.
It does not claim real-hardware performance.
What this is
A software-in-the-loop demonstration that Jean's deterministic architecture — with no training and no learned policy — decides whether, how hard, and when to act on a 6-DOF underwater vehicle in an independent simulator it did not author, holding station to 8 cm and refusing the impossible with zero false attempts.
What this is not
It is not a claim of real-hardware station keeping, nor of any platform-specific operational envelope, both of which remain future work with defined paths.
The method transfers; the coefficients do not.
Known boundaries
The operational envelope is REXROV's.
The drag curves were measured on an 1 862 kg work-class vehicle. Applying them to a 17 kg inspection-class ROV would be the same error this programme has already paid for. The method transfers; the coefficients do not.
Effective mass could not be measured.
With quadratic drag at 280 412 N/(m/s)², the vehicle reaches terminal velocity in about one second; mass governs only that window, and at the achievable ~10 Hz sample rate it contains roughly ten points. The estimator was validated on synthetic data and recovered known masses exactly, but railed against its search bound on the real plant. It is recorded as not identifiable and not required — the plant is governed by drag, and drag was measured well.
All refusals were caught at pre-flight.
The in-task abort path exists and is reachable, but Phase 4's faults were detectable before commitment. Mid-run fault injection is specified and unbuilt.
Position is odometry ground truth, not Jean's dead reckoning.
This was deliberate — it isolates the control law. Moving to her own estimate, with the estimate checked against truth every run, is the next step.

Democratizing AI
A world where humans and AI work together — on the problems that actually matter.
The current AI economy moves intelligence upward — into large clouds, behind enterprise contracts, accessible only to those with the infrastructure to reach it. That is not the only path forward.
Jean OS is built on a different premise: that intelligence belongs at the edge, in the hands of the people doing the work. A teacher in a rural classroom. A clinician in an under-resourced clinic. A conservationist in the field without reliable internet.
AI that runs locally doesn't just protect privacy — it democratizes capability. The same quality of intelligence that powers a Fortune 500 enterprise can run on a five-year-old laptop in a school that can barely afford textbooks.
That is the world we are building toward. Not AI over humans. Not humans resisting AI. Both, in harmony, working on things that actually matter.

For 20 years, Ayinde Rudolph served as a school administrator — nearly a decade of that as a superintendent, the person responsible when a system fails a child. He watched teachers burn out under administrative weight, watched students fall through gaps that technology promised to close but never did, and watched AI arrive and make the same mistake everyone else had: building for the data center instead of the classroom.
He returned to software development — after a 30-year gap — to build the thing he kept waiting for someone else to build. A local-first, privacy-preserving AI that runs entirely on the user's device. No cloud dependency. No data leaving the room. No vendor with a backdoor to your students' lives.
What started as a solution for education became something larger: a platform architecture that works across every regulated domain — medicine, defense, robotics, navigation — because the underlying problem is the same everywhere. The intelligence is in the wrong place. mYa Solutions puts it back where it belongs.

We determine whether a capability is real by first asking: is there an industry-standard Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) test for this domain? If yes, we run it and publish the methodology. If not, we define one, document the criteria, and hold ourselves to it. Boundary conditions are named. Failures are reported alongside successes. The result that survives a hostile reader is the only result worth showing.
Raw data — JSON trial reports, Criterion benchmark outputs — is available for independent verification on request. We don't hide the numbers that don't look perfect. We explain them.

sections.heading: The market just caught up to what we already built.
sections.summary: Why now  Sovereign AI, edge compute, and privacy-first software are now the fastest-growing segments in enterprise technology. We've been building this architecture since before those terms were headlines.
sections.text:
Why now
The market just caught up to what we already built.
Sovereign AI, edge compute, and privacy-first software are now the fastest-growing segments in enterprise technology. We've been building this architecture since before those terms were headlines.
01
Sovereign AI
Governments and enterprises worldwide are demanding AI that runs within their borders, on their hardware, under their control. Jean OS was designed for this from day one — not retrofitted to meet a regulation.
02
Edge compute
The shift from cloud-first to edge-first is accelerating. Jean's architecture is natively local — the edge is where it lives, not a deployment option added later.
03
Privacy by architecture
HIPAA, FERPA, CMMC, GDPR — regulated industries need AI that is private by construction, not by policy. Jean OS cannot exfiltrate data because it never touches a network to begin with.
04
Substrate invariance
One architecture. Five domains already proven. Every new domain we enter costs us less than the last — because we're not rebuilding, we're extending.
